catalog_quote: § 13. In words which have only two syllables the accent is always on the first : puddā, short; bāckā, word. In words of three syllables the verbs have generally the accent on the second syllable, tisignā to open, kirta'anā, to return; except in those which end in ba'anā, e.g., guchāba'anā, which take the accent on the third syllable. There are rare instances of verbs of three syllables having the accent on the first : nisigna, to dress a wound; nedegnā, to fall off, are examples. Adverbs, however, as a rule take the accent on the first syllable, even though they are of three or four syllables except when they are compounds, like nelbenjā, the day after to-morrow, mundbhāre, ahead, etc.; in these the accent is on the first syllable of the second word, that is the second syllable of the compound word. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: confirmed verbatim on the page image we hold of Hahn 1911 p. 9 sec. 13 and in the scanned text we hold; locator correct. sources.quote: 'In some disyllabic words the first syllable gets more prominence whereas in other words the second syllable gets more prominence.' Second-syllable accent: got-tˈa: (collective), tat-xˈa: 'mango', en-dˈe:r 'what', kat-ˈtʰən 'tale' -- 'for the above words the accent for the syllable is fixed'. First-syllable accent: mˈe:-nəi 'listen', ˈʧa:-de 'evening', xˈʌd-dar 'children' -- 'the first syllable is more prominent ... as in the first syllable the vowel is prolonged'. Trisyllables (ʧiʧ-ˈja:r-a: 'shout', er-ˈʧe:r-num 'sweat', po-ˈxa:-ri: 'pond', bid-put-ˈta: 'entire day', niŋ-ˈgi:-jo 'your mother'
